624.title: Hanuman makes himself small
624.hook: to comfort Sita, the monkey who just crossed an ocean calls himself the weakest of the army
624.carry: hanuman's humility: small self, big hope
624.howItsDone: Many Hindu families read the Sundara Kanda aloud in times of illness or trouble, and devotees love Hanuman as both the strongest and the humblest of Rama's servants; the chudamani is a familiar image in Ramayana art.

segments.voice: Yesterday: her doubt. Even when Hanuman grew like a mountain, Sita said no, for safety, choice and Rama's honor. Your line: maryada: the right way matters, not just the rescue.
screen: `MARYADA: THE RIGHT WAY MATTERS, NOT JUST THE RESCUE.`

segments.voice: Hanuman has to leave Sita in the grove. She's chosen to wait for Rama. Goodbyes like this are the hardest part: you're leaving, they're staying, and you want to say something that lasts after you've gone. Before he goes, she gives him tokens to take back, and he gives her something too: his counsel. A few sentences meant to hold her up until help arrives.
screen: `THE HARDEST PART IS THE GOODBYE.` → `TOKENS FOR RAMA.` → `COUNSEL FOR SITA.`

segments.voice: First, Sita's tokens. She tells Hanuman a private memory only Rama would know. One day at Chitrakuta a crow kept attacking her, and Rama, angry, sent a single blade of grass after it, charged with divine power; the crow found no shelter anywhere until it came back and fell at Rama's feet. Then she unties a jewel from her hair, the chudamani, and gives it to him. And she says plainly that she can hold on only for a month. Then Hanuman counsels her. Don't grieve. Rama and Lakshmana will come soon with Sugriva's army. And because Sita has asked how monkeys could ever cross this ocean, he adds something surprising. There are many in Sugriva's army stronger than me, and none weaker. If I could cross, how much more easily can they? The monkey who leapt a hundred yojanas calls himself the least of the army. If he's the strongest, the rescue hangs on one monkey. If he's the weakest, help is enormous, and coming. He makes himself small, so her hope can be large. This is the Hanuman devotees love most: the strongest one in the story, and the humblest. In Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas, when Rama later praises him, Hanuman says it was all Rama's power, none of his own. In Hindu devotion, humility means getting the ego out of the way so something bigger can come through. And it's one reason many families read this book, the Sundara Kanda, aloud when someone is sick or in trouble: it's the book where hope comes back.
screen: `THE CROW AND THE BLADE OF GRASS.` · `THE JEWEL FROM HER HAIR.` · `NONE IN THE ARMY IS WEAKER THAN ME.` · then, large: `SMALL SELF, BIG HOPE.`

segments.voice: If you pray, hold in mind someone waiting on something hard, a diagnosis, a result, a return, and say Hanuman's name or a short prayer for them, the way families read the Sundara Kanda for someone in trouble. If you don't pray, hold them in mind and let a few simple, true words of comfort form, shaped to what they most fear, not to what makes you look good. Breathe them slowly in and out.
Hanuman's counsel. His words to Sita before leaving: don't grieve, Rama will come, and there are many in the army stronger than me, and none weaker.
Your line: hanuman's humility: small self, big hope. Tomorrow, the strong one stops to think. Day six hundred twenty-four, done.

625.title: Strength and wisdom
625.hook: the job is done and Hanuman could fly home, but first he stops to think: the strength devotees pray to is strength with a mind
625.carry: bala, buddhi, vidya: strength needs wisdom
625.howItsDone: Many Hindus recite the Hanuman Chalisa, often on Tuesdays and Saturdays, and its opening asks Hanuman for strength, wisdom and knowledge; some teachers of the Sundara Kanda point to his deliberation in the grove as that wisdom at work.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Hanuman's counsel to Sita. He made himself the least of the army, so her hope could be big. Your line: Hanuman's humility, small self, big hope.

Hanuman has found Sita, delivered the ring, received the jewel. His mission, as Sugriva gave it, is complete. Going home now would be perfectly fair. Or there's the other question: while I'm here, is there something more this needs? He walks a little way from Sita through the grove, and Valmiki, once again, lets us hear him think it through.

His reasoning comes in steps. First: I've found Sita; that was the work I was given. But a little remains. Rama will have to fight Ravana, and it would help him to know the enemy's strength. Second, he runs through the four classic ways of dealing with an opponent in Indian statecraft: conciliation, gifts, division and force. Conciliation does no good with rakshasas. Gifts mean nothing to those already piled with wealth. People proud of their strength can't be split apart. Only force is left: a show of strength, to test them and to be brought before Ravana himself. Third, a principle. The one fit for a task gets many things done without working against the first. Sita is found, and nothing he does next can undo that. Only now does he allow himself the risk, and he decides to wreck Ravana's pleasure garden. Here's why this matters to Hindus. Hanuman isn't only muscle. Devotees love him as strength with a mind. The Hanuman Chalisa, the hymn many Hindus know by heart, opens with a prayer: knowing I lack understanding, I remember the son of the wind; give me bala, buddhi, vidya. Strength, wisdom, knowledge. It calls him learned, good and very clever, eager to do Rama's work. That's the teaching: devotion doesn't switch the mind off. Power without wisdom is Ravana. Power with wisdom, offered to Rama, is Hanuman.
screen: `THE TASK IS DONE; A LITTLE REMAINS.` · `ONLY FORCE IS LEFT.` · `STRENGTH WITH A MIND.` · then, large: `BALA, BUDDHI, VIDYA: STRENGTH NEEDS WISDOM.`

segments.voice: If you pray, ask Hanuman in your own words, or with the Chalisa's own line if you know it, for what it asks: strength, wisdom and knowledge. Then bring to mind one thing you face this week that needs all three, and ask for all three. If you don't pray, picture that same task and ask yourself honestly: where am I pushing when I need to think? Breathe slowly, and let the plan settle before you act.

626.title: Rama's servant
626.hook: a monkey tears up Ravana's favorite garden, leaving one tree standing, and then announces exactly whose servant he is
626.carry: dasya bhakti: i am rama's servant
626.howItsDone: Hanuman's declaration of victory to Rama and of himself as Rama's servant is recited by devotees, and some see in it the heart of Hanuman's devotion, dāsya, the love of a servant.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Hanuman's counsel with himself. He thought before he struck, the task secure, the four ways weighed. Your line: bala, buddhi, vidya: strength needs wisdom.

At dawn, the birds of the ashoka grove start up in alarm. Trees crash down. Pools are churned to mud. Pavilions come apart. Ravana's most beautiful garden is being taken apart by something huge. The guards wake, and they notice something odd. In the middle of the wreckage, one tree is left untouched: the one Sita sits beneath.
screen: `DAWN, AND THE GROVE COMES DOWN.` → `ONE TREE LEFT STANDING.`

segments.voice: The rakshasi guards turn to Sita. Who is that? What did he say to you? Sita gives a clever answer. How would I know? Rakshasas are the ones who change shape at will. You'd know better than I would. She protects Hanuman and gives them nothing. The guards run to Ravana, who sends a great company of armed servants to capture the monkey. Hanuman is waiting for them on the gateway arch. He grows huge, slaps his arms, and roars a declaration, which Valmiki gives in full. Victory to Rama, mighty in strength, and to Lakshmana. Victory to King Sugriva. And then: dāso 'haṃ kosalendrasya. I am the servant of the lord of Kosala, Rama. I am Hanuman, son of the wind. Notice the order. In the enemy's capital, at the start of a fight, he says whose servant he is before he says who he is. Hindus have a name for this love: dasya bhakti, loving God as a servant loves a master he adores. It's why, in so many Hindu homes and temples, the picture of Rama's court shows Hanuman kneeling at Rama's feet, hands folded. The strongest one in the room chooses the lowest place, and devotees see that as his greatness, not his weakness. Then the servants rush him. Hanuman snatches up an iron bar from the gateway and drives them back. It's only the first wave. Lanka is about to show him its strength.
screen: `ONE TREE, AND SITA, SPARED.` · `HOW WOULD I KNOW?` · `I AM THE SERVANT OF RAMA.` · then, large: `DASYA BHAKTI: THE LOVE OF A SERVANT.`

segments.voice: If you have a family shrine or a picture of Hanuman, fold your hands and say softly, Jai Shri Ram, or simply Rama's name, putting him first the way Hanuman did. If you don't pray, ask yourself gently: what do I serve and love, a family, a craft, a friend, a good? Name it before you name anything about yourself, and breathe with it.
The fight. Hanuman wrecks Ravana's grove but spares Sita's tree, declares himself Rama's servant from the gateway, and drives back the first wave of guards.
Your line: dasya bhakti: i am rama's servant. Tomorrow, Lanka sends its best. See you then.

627.title: Bound, by choice
627.hook: Hanuman beats every champion Lanka sends, until a god's weapon binds him, and the enemy's own ropes undo it
627.carry: shraddha: trust given whole, not halfway
627.howItsDone: Hanuman bound by Indrajit's Brahmastra appears in recitations and dance-dramas, and some teachers of the Sundara Kanda use the ropes that undo the divine weapon to talk about shraddha, wholehearted faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the grove came down, one tree spared, and at the gate Hanuman called himself Rama's servant. Your line: dasya bhakti, I am Rama's servant.

Ravana keeps raising the stakes. After the first wave falls, he sends Jambumali, a fierce warrior. Then seven sons of his ministers, in shining chariots. Then five of his generals. Each time the same news comes back to the palace: the monkey is still on the gate. Then Ravana sends his own young son, Aksha, and Valmiki pauses the fighting to let Hanuman look at the boy.
screen: `JAMBUMALI, THE SEVEN, THE FIVE.` → `THEN RAVANA'S YOUNG SON.`

segments.voice: Hanuman admires Aksha; Valmiki tells us so. The boy is brave and skilled, radiant like the young sun, and Hanuman is reluctant to kill one so young. But Aksha's arrows keep coming, and he decides an enemy this strong can't be ignored. The epic doesn't hide the cost. Now Ravana sends his son Indrajit, whose name means conqueror of Indra. Their duel is long, and neither can wound the other. So Indrajit reaches for the weapon of Brahma, the Brahmastra, and binds Hanuman with it. Hanuman falls. And he knows this weapon: by Brahma's own blessing, it can hold him only a short while. He chooses to stay down, out of respect for Brahma, and because it serves his purpose: to be brought before Ravana. Then comes the detail teachers love. The rakshasas aren't content to leave him in the god's weapon. They tie him with ropes and bark of their own, and Valmiki says the Brahmastra lets go the moment other bonds are added. Indrajit despairs; his own soldiers have undone his weapon. Some devotional teachers read this as a lesson in shraddha, faith given whole: a sacred bond doesn't share the job with doubt. On that reading, the scene shows two kinds of trust. The rakshasas hedge, and lose their hold. Hanuman honors the god and trusts the moment to carry him where Rama needs him. He lets them drag him through the streets into the hall where Ravana sits.
screen: `HANUMAN HESITATES OVER AKSHA.` · `INDRAJIT AND THE BRAHMASTRA.` · `ROPES ADDED; THE WEAPON LETS GO.` · then, large: `SHRADDHA: TRUST GIVEN WHOLE.`

628.title: The fire that didn't burn
628.hook: a messenger gives the most powerful king in the world good advice, and the king answers by setting the messenger's tail on fire
628.carry: sita's prayer: holding someone up from afar
628.howItsDone: The burning of Hanuman's tail and Sita's prayer to Agni are familiar scenes in Ramayana retellings; many Hindu families light a diya at home and pray for someone ill or far away, and Vibhishana's rule that an envoy must not be killed is cited by some teachers as dharma in war.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the fight went on, and the rakshasas' doubting ropes undid a god's weapon. Your line: shraddha: trust given whole, not halfway.

Hanuman stands tied up before Ravana's throne, and the first thing Valmiki tells us is that Hanuman is impressed. Ravana is magnificent: radiant, crowned, mighty, surrounded by ministers. Hanuman thinks that if this king weren't so unrighteous, he could be the guardian of heaven itself. A minister asks who sent him, and Hanuman answers. Not with threats. With counsel.
screen: `HANUMAN IS IMPRESSED.` → `IF ONLY HE WERE RIGHTEOUS.` → `NOT THREATS, COUNSEL.`

segments.voice: I am Sugriva's envoy, he says, and Rama's messenger. Then he speaks to Ravana as to a king who could still choose well. You know dharma. You've gained great power through austerities. Don't throw it away for another man's wife. Give Sita back to Rama, and you can still live. Ravana's answer is rage: kill him. Then his younger brother Vibhishana speaks up. It is against dharma to kill a messenger. Punish him some other way. Ravana gives in, grudgingly. A monkey's tail is precious to him, he says. Set it on fire. So they wrap Hanuman's tail in old cloth, soak it in oil, light it, and parade him through the streets with drums. The rakshasi guards run to tell Sita. And Sita, in the grove, turns to the fire god, Agni. If I have served my husband faithfully, she prays, if I have any merit at all, be cool to Hanuman. The fire, burning brightly on his tail, does not burn him. Hanuman is astonished, and guesses it's Sita's doing, or Rama's power, or his father the wind's friendship with fire. Look at Sita here. She can't reach Hanuman. She can't fight for him. She can only pray from where she sits, and in the story, that holds him up. This is one of the quiet practices of Hindu life: praying for someone you can't reach, often with a small lamp lit at home for someone far away or in a hospital.
screen: `RETURN SITA AND BE SAVED.` · `AN ENVOY MAY NOT BE KILLED.` · `SITA PRAYS TO AGNI FROM AFAR.` · then, large: `THE FIRE DOES NOT BURN HIM.`

segments.voice: If you pray, light a small lamp or candle, or simply fold your hands, and name someone going through a fire right now: an illness, a hard week, a trial. Sita couldn't go to Hanuman; she prayed from where she was. Offer them to God in your own way. If you don't pray, send them coolness and steadiness with each breath out, and then send them a real message if you can.
The burning. Ravana rejects Hanuman's counsel, Vibhishana saves the envoy's life, and Hanuman's tail is set alight, but Sita asks the fire to be cool, and it is.
Your line: sita's prayer: holding someone up from afar. Tomorrow, the fire spreads across Lanka. Rest well.

629.title: Anger, shed like a skin
629.hook: Lanka goes up in flames, and the monkey who lit it stands on the shore suddenly sick with one question: what if Sita burned too?
629.carry: krodha: shed anger like a snake's skin
629.howItsDone: Lanka-dahana, the burning of Lanka, is a beloved scene in Ramlila performances and temple art, and Hanuman's self-reproach over anger afterward is often quoted by teachers as a lesson in self-control.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the burning began. Sita prayed from the grove, and the fire didn't burn Hanuman. Your line: sita's prayer: holding someone up from afar.

Hanuman leaps from rooftop to rooftop with his blazing tail, and the wind, his father, fans every flame. Mansions, towers and gateways catch fire. Valmiki describes Lanka burning like the end of an age. Then Hanuman dips his tail in the sea, stops, and looks back. It's the moment after anger, when the heat drains away and a cold thought arrives: what did I just break?
screen: `LANKA BURNS.` → `HE LOOKS BACK.` → `THE MOMENT AFTER ANGER.`

segments.voice: Valmiki notes one careful detail. Hanuman spares one house in all of Lanka: Vibhishana's, the brother who spoke up for him. Then the cold thought. Sita. Did the fire reach the grove? Did I burn the very person I came to save? Hanuman is horrified, and he turns on his own anger with words worth keeping. Blessed is the one who can throw off anger the moment it rises, the way a snake sheds its old skin. An angry person can do anything: harm a teacher, say what should never be said. He calls himself a fool who has ruined Rama's whole mission in a moment of fury. The hero of the Sundara Kanda, at the height of his triumph, condemns his own temper. This is a teaching Hindus hear again and again. Anger, krodha, is counted among the six inner enemies, the shadripu, along with desire, greed, delusion, pride and envy: enemies you fight inside, not outside. Then Hanuman hears the charanas, celestial beings, marveling in the sky: Lanka is burned, and yet Janaki, Sita, is unharmed. Relief floods him, and he sees why: Sita is guarded by her own power. Fire, he reasons, does not burn fire. He goes back one last time to the ashoka grove, sees her alive with his own eyes, bows, and takes his leave. He doesn't stay stuck in shame. He sheds the anger and goes to make sure she's safe.
screen: `VIBHISHANA'S HOUSE IS SPARED.` · `WHAT IF SITA BURNED?` · `KRODHA, AN INNER ENEMY.` · `LIKE A SNAKE SHEDDING ITS SKIN.` · then, large: `SITA IS UNHARMED.`

segments.voice: Recall a recent moment of anger, small or large, and without reliving the argument, notice where you feel it in the body: jaw, chest, hands. Breathe into that place, and on each breath out let the anger loosen and slip off, the way a snake slides out of an old skin. If you pray, say Rama's name softly as it goes. Then, like Hanuman going back to the grove, think of one step to set things right.
The burning. Lanka set ablaze, Vibhishana's house spared, Hanuman's horror at his own anger, and the voices that tell him Sita is unharmed.
Your line: krodha: shed anger like a snake's skin. Tomorrow, the leap home. Day six hundred twenty-nine.

630.title: Hope comes home
630.hook: on the far shore, a waiting army hears a roar over the sea, and knows from the sound alone that Sita is found
630.carry: sundara kanda: the book where hope returns
630.howItsDone: Many Hindu families read the Sundara Kanda aloud in hard times or to fulfil a vow, often finishing with prasad shared around, and the return of Hanuman and the monkeys' joy on Mount Mahendra is read with delight.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the burning of Lanka, and Hanuman turning on his own anger. Your line: krodha: shed anger like a snake's skin.

On the northern shore, Angada, Jambavan and the whole search party have been waiting, watching the sea the way people watch the doors at an arrivals gate, trying to read a face before it reaches them. Then they hear it. A roar, far off over the water, getting louder. Jambavan listens and says: that's the roar of someone who has succeeded.
screen: `WATCHING THE SEA.` → `A ROAR OVER THE WATER.` → `THE SOUND OF SUCCESS.`

segments.voice: The flight back begins like the first one. Hanuman climbs a mountain on Lanka's shore, Arishta, and presses down to spring; Valmiki says the mountain sinks into the earth. Then he's in the air, and Valmiki makes the sky an ocean: the moon a water lily, the sun a waterbird, the clouds its water weed. Nearing Mahendra, he roars, so the others will know before he lands. They hear, and they know. The monkeys leap from tree to tree, waving branches, delirious. Hanuman lands among them, and they crowd around him with fruit and roots, cheering. He bows to Jambavan and Angada and tells them in a few words: I've seen her. She's alive. Then, at Jambavan's urging, he tells them everything, from the beginning. And that brings us near the end of the Sundara Kanda, the fifth book of the Ramayana. Sundara means beautiful, and teachers give different reasons for the name. But ask Hindu families why they read it, and you'll often hear: it's the book of hope. It begins with Sita lost and a search party that nearly gave up. Its last chapters carry the news home over the sea: she's alive. That's why many families read it aloud when someone is ill or in trouble, and finish the reading with prasad, sweets offered to God and shared. Hope, in this book, isn't wishful thinking. It's a devoted servant who crossed the sea, and came back with the news.
screen: `ARISHTA SINKS AS HE LEAPS.` · `I'VE SEEN HER. SHE'S ALIVE.` · `THE BOOK OF HOPE.` · then, large: `THE BOOK WHERE HOPE RETURNS.`

segments.voice: If you pray, read a few lines of the Sundara Kanda or the Hanuman Chalisa for someone you love who's waiting on news, or simply say Hanuman's name for them. If you don't pray, remember a time someone came home with good news, and the moment before the words when their face already told you. Breathe in that relief, and let the breath go out slowly, as if you were landing.
The return. Hanuman's leap back from Mount Arishta, his roar over the sea, and the search party who know, from the sound alone, that he has found Sita.
